exam: A patient with CD4 150 cells/µL presents with headache and papilledema – what is the most urgent investigation and why? — Perform lumbar puncture with opening pressure measurement; high pressure suggests cryptococcal meningitis requiring immediate antifungal therapy.

You have a febrile HIV patient with dry cough and diffuse infiltrates on chest X‑ray; sputum is negative for bacteria. Which test would you order next and what result would confirm PCP? — Order induced sputum or BAL for PCR or silver stain; detection of Pneumocystis organisms confirms PCP.

A child with sickle cell disease develops fever, weight loss and night sweats; TB is suspected but GeneXpert is unavailable. How do you proceed? — Start empirical anti‑TB therapy based on clinical criteria and monitor response; obtain sputum smear if possible.

Why is fluconazole alone insufficient for initial treatment of cryptococcal meningitis? — It is fungistatic; initial fungicidal amphotericin B reduces mortality, with fluconazole used for consolidation.
What prophylactic medication reduces the risk of both PCP and toxoplasmosis in HIV, and when should it be started? — Trimethoprim‑sulfamethoxazole; start when CD4 < 200 cells/µL.

A patient on ganciclovir for CMV retinitis develops severe neutropenia. What alternative can you use and why? — Switch to oral valganciclovir if tolerated; it has similar efficacy with less marrow suppression.
Explain why a normal CD4 count during acute malaria may be misleading in an HIV patient. — Acute infection can cause transient lymphocytosis, falsely elevating CD4; repeat after malaria treatment.

During a ward round you encounter a patient with unexplained anaemia, diarrhoea and weight loss; CD4 is 180 cells/µL. Which opportunistic infection should be high on your list and what test would you order? — Consider disseminated Mycobacterium avium complex; order blood culture for MAC and consider abdominal ultrasound for organomegaly.
ai.title: Opportunistic Infections in Immunocompromised Patients
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Opportunistic infections arise when weakened immunity permits normally harmless microbes to cause disease. Recognising patterns, risk factors and limited diagnostics in low‑resource settings guides timely treatment.

b: Diagnosis relies on clinical syndrome plus targeted microbiology or imaging, often using syndromic algorithms when labs are unavailable.
sections.p: Infections that occur in patients with impaired cell‑mediated immunity, most commonly advanced HIV, but also TB, malnutrition, chronic steroid use, or hematologic malignancy.

b: Stage III: weight loss >10 %, chronic diarrhoea, pulmonary TB, severe bacterial pneumonia.
Stage IV: cryptococcal meningitis, disseminated Mycobacterium avium complex, Kaposi sarcoma, CMV retinitis.
sections.p: Severity is graded by the WHO HIV clinical stage (III–IV) and by organ dysfunction (e.g., respiratory failure, encephalopathy).

b: HIV/AIDS – CD4 < 200 cells/µL.
Tuberculosis – pulmonary and extrapulmonary.
Cryptococcus neoformans – meningitis.
Pneumocystis jirovecii – pneumonia.
CMV – retinitis, colitis, oesophagitis.
Mycobacterium avium complex – disseminated disease.
Histoplasma capsulatum – disseminated histoplasmosis.
Severe malaria or schistosomiasis with co‑infection.
sections.p: Common opportunists in East Africa and similar low‑resource settings:

b: Subacute fever, weight loss, night sweats – TB or MAC.
Progressive dyspnoea, dry cough, hypoxia – PCP.
Headache, neck stiffness, photophobia – cryptococcal meningitis.
Blurred vision, floaters – CMV retinitis.
Diarrhoea, abdominal pain – CMV colitis or intestinal TB.
sections.p: Presentations reflect the organ involved and the pathogen’s typical syndrome.

t.b: Immunosuppression level; <200 cells/µL predicts most OIs — guides prophylaxis.
Detects Mycobacterium tuberculosis; positive confirms pulmonary TB — start first‑line therapy.
Identifies Cryptococcus capsular yeast; positive confirms cryptococcal meningitis — start amphotericin B + fluconazole.

t.a: Serum (1‑3)-β‑D‑glucan or PCR for Pneumocystis (if available)
t.b: Supports PCP diagnosis when bronchoalveolar lavage not possible — start high‑dose cotrimoxazole.
Detects CMV retinitis; lesions with haemorrhage confirm diagnosis — start systemic ganciclovir.

t.a: Full blood count and liver function
t.b: Baseline for drug toxicity monitoring; anemia or transaminase rise may limit therapy.

b: Cryptococcal meningitis – intracranial pressure >250 mmH₂O.
PCP – PaO₂ < 70 mmHg on room air.
Disseminated TB – multi‑organ failure.
sections.p: Rapid deterioration, altered mental status, severe hypoxia, or uncontrolled sepsis demand urgent referral.

b: First‑line anti‑TB regimen (rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, ethambutol) – kills Mycobacterium tuberculosis; avoid fluoroquinolones if QT prolongation risk.
Amphotericin B + fluconazole for cryptococcal meningitis – fungicidal then consolidation; avoid nephrotoxic drugs concurrently.
High‑dose cotrimoxazole for PCP – covers Pneumocystis; avoid sulfa allergy.
Ganciclovir for CMV disease – antiviral; avoid in severe neutropenia.
Adjunctive steroids for TB meningitis and severe PCP (if hypoxic).
Start or optimise antiretroviral therapy after acute OI control (usually 2–8 weeks).
sections.p: Treat the specific pathogen, provide supportive care, and address immune restoration where possible.

b: Trimethoprim‑sulfamethoxazole prophylaxis for CD4 < 200 cells/µL – prevents PCP, toxoplasmosis, some bacterial infections.
Fluconazole secondary prophylaxis after cryptococcal meningitis until CD4 > 200 cells/µL for 6 months.
Vaccination (pneumococcal, hepatitis B) where available.
Nutritional support and treatment of co‑existing malaria or schistosomiasis.
sections.p: Regular clinical review, CD4 monitoring, and prophylaxis reduce recurrence.

b: Bacterial pneumonia – presents with productive cough, lobar consolidation; OI pneumonia often dry cough, diffuse infiltrates.
Tuberculous meningitis – similar CSF profile; cryptococcal meningitis shows India‑Ink positive yeast.
Negative sputum smear does not rule out TB in HIV; consider GeneXpert or clinical trial of therapy.
Normal CD4 count in acute infection may be falsely high; repeat after stabilisation.
CSF glucose may be normal in early cryptococcal meningitis; rely on India‑Ink.

whenToSeekHelp: Altered consciousness, seizures, or focal neurological signs
Severe dyspnoea with SpO₂ < 90 % on room air
